questions.q: A handler does const a = await getSales(); const b = await getRefunds();. Each service takes 100 ms and neither needs the other's result. About how long does the handler wait, and what is this shape called?
questions.explain: Each await waits before the next request even starts, so the times add up. Independent requests should start together and be awaited together.

questions.q: When does a promise's work start? What does this print?
questions.explain: Calling an async function runs it until its first await straight away. Both loads started before await a, so they ran at the same time. await only waits for work that is already happening.
options: start sales, start refunds, both created, end sales, end refunds
both created, start sales, end sales, start refunds, end refunds
start sales, end sales, start refunds, end refunds, both created
start sales, start refunds, end sales, end refunds, both created

questions.q: Why is const a = loadA(); const b = loadB(); try { use(await a, await b); } catch {} risky when both can fail?
questions.explain: Only the promise currently being awaited has a handler. A combinator like Promise.all attaches handlers to every input immediately, so no rejection is left unhandled.
options: The two loads run one after another
If b rejects while the code is still waiting on a, b has no handler yet, which is an unhandled rejection
await cannot be used twice in one expression
The catch block catches both errors twice

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Promise.all keeps the input order, whichever finishes first. A plain value like "stock" counts as an already-fulfilled promise.

questions.q: An order with no items is processed. What does this print?
questions.explain: Promise.all([]) fulfils immediately with an empty array. Compare Promise.race([]), which never settles, and Promise.any([]), which rejects.
options: TypeError: Promise.all needs at least one promise

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Promise.all rejects with the first rejection in time, not the first in the array. The price service failed at 10 ms, before the stock service at 30 ms.
options: stock service down, price service down

questions.q: Promise.all([chargeCard(), sendConfirmationEmail()]) rejects because the card is declined. What happens to the email?
questions.explain: A promise is a receipt for work that is already running. Promise.all can stop waiting, but it cannot stop the work. Side effects that depend on a check must run after the check, or be cancellable.
options: It still runs to completion; only its result is ignored

questions.q: Why might a team prefer an allNamed({ sales, refunds }) helper returning an object over const [sales, refunds] = await Promise.all([...])?
questions.explain: Positional destructuring depends on two lists staying in the same order. Names make the mapping explicit. It is still Promise.all underneath, with the same fail-fast behaviour.
options: It cancels the other promises on failure
Results are matched by name, so reordering the inputs cannot silently swap values

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each report has status: "fulfilled" with a value, or "rejected" with a reason. allSettled itself never rejects.

questions.q: When does the promise returned by Promise.allSettled reject?
questions.explain: That is why you must check every report's status yourself: failures are data now, not exceptions. And because it waits for every input, a very slow one holds everything.
options: Never; it fulfils once every input has settled
When an input takes longer than 30 seconds

questions.q: A dashboard uses allSettled over five widgets. One widget's service sometimes hangs for 30 seconds. What should you add?
questions.explain: allSettled waits for the slowest input. Wrapping each promise in withTimeout turns "too slow" into an ordinary rejection that the dashboard can show as unavailable.
options: Nothing, allSettled already skips slow promises
A time limit on each widget's promise, so a slow one becomes a rejection

questions.q: Which combinator fits "show every widget that loaded, and mark the rest as unavailable"?
questions.explain: Partial results are useful here, so you need a report for each widget. all would lose every result on the first failure; race and any give only one result.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: race settles like the first input to settle, success or failure. The rejection came first. For "first success", use Promise.any.

questions.q: What does await Promise.race([]) do?
questions.explain: An empty race never settles. If the list of promises comes from data, check that it is not empty, or the request hangs.
options: Waits forever: with no inputs, nothing can ever win

questions.q: withTimeout(chargeCard(order), 3000) rejects with a TimeoutError. What do you know about the payment?
questions.explain: A timeout stops waiting, not the work. The provider may charge the card after you gave up. Record "unknown", query the status, and use an idempotency key so a retry cannot charge twice.
options: It failed; tell the customer to try again
It was cancelled by the timeout
Its status is unknown: the request may still complete, so check with the provider before charging again
It succeeded, because timeouts only happen on success

questions.q: Why does withTimeout call clearTimeout(timer) in finally?
questions.explain: If the work wins, the timer still counts down. In a server that handles thousands of requests, each would leave a timer behind. finally clears it whichever side won.
options: To cancel the payment when it is slow
So the timer does not stay pending after the race is over, holding resources and keeping a Node.js process alive
Because race rejects if the timer is still running

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The rates arrived after 10 ms, before the 50 ms limit. The stock would take 80 ms but the limit was 20 ms, so the timer's rejection won the race.
options:
rates timed out
stock timed out

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: any ignores failures and takes the first success in time. mirror-a failed first and was skipped; mirror-c succeeded at 20 ms, before mirror-b at 30 ms.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: When every input fails, any rejects with an AggregateError whose errors array follows the input order, not the order of failure.

questions.q: What does Promise.any([]) do?
questions.explain: No input can succeed, so any rejects at once. Only race hangs on an empty list; all and allSettled fulfil with [].
options: Rejects straight away with an AggregateError

questions.q: Three exchange-rate providers can answer; any one answer is fine and you want the fastest working one. Which combinator?
questions.explain: Redundant sources are what any is for. race would fail as soon as the fastest provider returned an error, even if another would succeed a moment later.

questions.q: What does Promise.withResolvers() return?
questions.explain: It is the same as creating a promise with new Promise and copying resolve and reject out of the executor. It suits one-off events, such as waiting for a payment webhook.
options: A promise that is already fulfilled
An object { promise, resolve, reject }, so other code can settle the promise later
An array of the resolve functions of every pending promise
A function that resolves any promise passed to it

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The promise settles once, with the first resolve. The duplicate webhook's resolve is ignored, which is handy: providers do sometimes send the same webhook twice.
options:
waiting
webhook: order 7 paid
webhook: order 7 paid again

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Promise.try(fn, ...args) calls fn and always returns a promise. A synchronous throw becomes a rejection, so one .catch handles both kinds of failure.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: forEach calls the async callback for each item and ignores the promises it returns, so it finishes before any email is sent. Use for...of with await for sequential work, or Promise.all(items.map(fn)) for parallel work.
options: TypeError: forEach does not accept async functions

questions.q: Which job should run strictly one item at a time?
questions.explain: When each step depends on the result of the step before, the work must be sequential. Running those posts in parallel creates a race condition: overlapping reads and writes lose entries.
options: Fetching the prices of ten products
Posting a list of ledger entries where each entry's balance depends on the previous one
Asking three mirrors for the same file

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both sales read 10 before either wrote. The first wrote 8, then the second overwrote it with 10 - 3 = 7. One sale was lost. Read-then-write on shared state must not overlap: run such updates sequentially, or make the update itself atomic.

questions.q: Why is await Promise.all(customers.map(sendEmail)) dangerous when customers comes from the database?
questions.explain: Parallelism must be bounded when the list size is not under your control. Use batches or a pool with a fixed limit, which the concurrency lesson builds.
options: Promise.all cannot take more than 1,000 promises
It starts every send at once; with 100,000 customers that overwhelms the mail server or your rate limit
The emails are sent in random order
map does not work with async functions

questions.q: Emails are sent in batches of 5 with Promise.all per batch. One email in a batch takes 5 seconds, the others 100 ms. What is wasted?
questions.explain: A batch finishes with its slowest item. A pool starts the next job as soon as any slot is free, which keeps all slots busy.
options: For almost 5 seconds only one email is in flight, while four slots sit empty waiting for the batch to finish
The slow email is sent five times
The next batch starts before the slow email finishes

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: slice past the end just returns what is left, so the last batch has one item. The results of all batches are collected into one flat array of 5.

questions.q: In the dashboard build, Promise.all([account, Promise.allSettled(widgets)]) is used. When can this Promise.all reject?
questions.explain: Nesting combinators expresses the rules: the account is required (its failure fails the page), the widgets are optional (their failures become reports).
options: Only when the account promise rejects, because allSettled never rejects

questions.q: A service keeps a Map from order id to the resolve/reject of a waiting promise. What must it also do?
questions.explain: A map holds its entries until you delete them. Without cleanup and a timeout for webhooks that never arrive, it is a slow memory leak.
options: Nothing; resolved entries are removed automatically
Delete each entry once its promise settles, and put a time limit on the wait, or the map grows forever
Resolve every entry twice to be sure
Store the promises in an array instead

questions.q: Load the product, its reviews and its stock in parallel (they are independent) and print the lines shown. The services count how many requests are in flight at once.
questions.explain: Start all three calls inside one Promise.all and destructure the results in input order. All three requests are in flight together, so the page waits for one round instead of three.
questions.expected:
Rice 5kg: 3 reviews, 12 in stock
requests in flight at once: 3

questions.q: Load all widgets with Promise.allSettled. Print each widget as NAME: VALUE or NAME: unavailable (REASON).
questions.explain: Keep the names in an array so report i can be matched to widget i, then branch on status.

questions.q: Finish withTimeout(promise, ms, label): it rejects with an error named TimeoutError and message LABEL timed out after MS ms if the promise takes longer, and clears its timer either way.
questions.explain: Race the work against a timer that rejects, and clear the timer in finally. Setting error.name lets callers tell a timeout from a real failure.
questions.expected:
paid
TimeoutError: payment timed out after 30 ms

questions.q: Use Promise.any to get the first working exchange rate. If every provider fails, print no rates: followed by the reasons joined with , .
questions.explain: any skips failures and takes the first success. When all fail, the AggregateError's errors array holds every reason in input order.
questions.expected:
c: 1538
no rates: a down, b down

questions.q: The ledger entries must be posted one after another, or entries are lost. Replace the forEach so the final balance is right.
questions.explain: forEach starts every post at once and does not wait; they all read the starting balance. for...of with await finishes each post before starting the next.

questions.q: Write allNamed(tasks): it takes an object whose values are promises and resolves to an object with the same keys and the resolved values.
questions.explain: Object.keys and Object.values return the entries in the same order, and Promise.all keeps that order, so name i matches value i.

questions.q: Finish waitForConfirmation(orderId) with Promise.withResolvers: store the resolve in waiting under the order id, return the promise, and delete the entry once it settles.
questions.explain: The webhook handler and the waiting code share the promise's resolve through the map. finally removes the entry so the map does not grow forever.
